solution: Split the integrand into powers of \(x\) before integrating: \(\dfrac{x + 1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{1/2} + x^{-1/2}\). By the fundamental theorem of integral calculus, \(\int_{1}^{9}\left(x^{1/2} + x^{-1/2}\right) dx = \left[\dfrac{2}{3} x^{3/2} + 2\sqrt{x}\right]_{1}^{9}\). At \(x = 9\) the bracket is \(\dfrac{2}{3}(27) + 2(3) = 24\), and at \(x = 1\) it is \(\dfrac{2}{3} + 2 = \dfrac{8}{3}\). \(\therefore\) the value of the integral is \(24 - \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{64}{3} \approx 21.33\).

Factorise the denominator and use partial fractions: \(x^{2} + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3)\) and \(\dfrac{1}{(x + 2)(x + 3)} = \dfrac{1}{x + 2} - \dfrac{1}{x + 3}\). Hence \(\int_{2}^{3} \dfrac{dx}{x^{2} + 5x + 6} = \left[\log\left|\dfrac{x + 2}{x + 3}\right|\right]_{2}^{3}\), the integrand being continuous on \([2, 3]\). Substituting the limits gives \(\log\dfrac{5}{6} - \log\dfrac{4}{5}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\log\dfrac{25}{24} \approx 0.04082\).

[Textbook misprint: the integral is printed as \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\cot^{2}x\) with no \(dx\), and as printed it DIVERGES: \(\cot^{2}x\sim 1/x^{2}\) at the lower limit, and the partial integrals \(\int_{\varepsilon}^{\pi/4}\) measure 98.2, 998.2, 9998.2, 99998.2 for \(\varepsilon=10^{-2}\ldots10^{-5}\), matching \(1/\varepsilon-1-\pi/4\) exactly. Both standard repairs — integrand \(\tan^{2}x\) on \([0,\pi/4]\), or \(\cot^{2}x\) on \([\pi/4,\pi/2]\) — give \(1-\pi/4\).]

This item is printed without a \(dx\), unlike every other question in the group, so the evident reading is \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \cot^{2} x \, dx\). Writing \(\cot^{2} x = \operatorname{cosec}^{2} x - 1\) gives the antiderivative \(-\cot x - x\), so \(\int_{\varepsilon}^{\pi/4} \cot^{2} x \, dx = \left[-\cot x - x\right]_{\varepsilon}^{\pi/4} = \left(-1 - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) + \cot\varepsilon + \varepsilon\), and since \(\cot\varepsilon \to \infty\) as \(\varepsilon \to 0^{+}\) the integral as printed DIVERGES, the integrand behaving like \(\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\) at the lower limit. The item is therefore defective as printed, and the defect is confined to a single misprint. Both standard repairs, namely reading the integrand as \(\tan^{2} x\) on \([0, \pi/4]\), or keeping \(\cot^{2} x\) with limits \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) to \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), give the same value, \(\left[\tan x - x\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = 1 - \dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.2146\), which is the intended answer.

Rationalise by multiplying numerator and denominator by \(1 + \sin x\): \(\dfrac{1}{1 - \sin x} = \dfrac{1 + \sin x}{1 - \sin^{2} x} = \dfrac{1 + \sin x}{\cos^{2} x} = \sec^{2} x + \sec x \tan x\), which is continuous on \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\). The antiderivative is \(\tan x + \sec x\), so the integral is \(\left[\tan x + \sec x\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\). At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) this is \(1 + \sqrt{2}\) and at \(x = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) it is \(-1 + \sqrt{2}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \((1 + \sqrt{2}) - (\sqrt{2} - 1) = 2\).

Rationalise the denominator by multiplying above and below by \(\sqrt{2x + 3} + \sqrt{2x - 3}\); since \((2x + 3) - (2x - 3) = 6\), the integrand becomes \(\dfrac{1}{6}\left(\sqrt{2x + 3} + \sqrt{2x - 3}\right)\). Using \(\int (2x \pm 3)^{1/2} dx = \dfrac{1}{3}(2x \pm 3)^{3/2}\), the integral equals \(\dfrac{1}{18}\left[(2x + 3)^{3/2} + (2x - 3)^{3/2}\right]_{3}^{5}\). At \(x = 5\) the bracket is \(13^{3/2} + 7^{3/2} = 13\sqrt{13} + 7\sqrt{7}\), and at \(x = 3\) it is \(9^{3/2} + 3^{3/2} = 27 + 3\sqrt{3}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{1}{18}\left(13\sqrt{13} + 7\sqrt{7} - 27 - 3\sqrt{3}\right) \approx 1.844\).

Since the degree of the numerator is not less than that of the denominator, divide first: \(\dfrac{x^{2} - 2}{x^{2} + 1} = \dfrac{(x^{2} + 1) - 3}{x^{2} + 1} = 1 - \dfrac{3}{x^{2} + 1}\). Hence \(\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x^{2} - 2}{x^{2} + 1} dx = \left[x - 3\tan^{-1} x\right]_{0}^{1}\). At \(x = 1\) this is \(1 - 3\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\) and at \(x = 0\) it is \(0\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(1 - \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \approx -1.356\); it is negative because \(x^{2} - 2 < 0\) throughout \([0, 1]\).

Convert the product into a sum using \(2\sin A \sin B = \cos(A - B) - \cos(A + B)\), so \(\sin 4x \sin 3x = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\cos x - \cos 7x\right)\). Then \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \sin 4x \sin 3x \, dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\sin x - \dfrac{\sin 7x}{7}\right]_{0}^{\pi/4}\). At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), giving \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{1}{7\sqrt{2}}\right)\); the lower limit contributes \(0\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{8}{7\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{7} \approx 0.4041\).

Recognise the perfect square \(1 + \sin 2x = \sin^{2} x + \cos^{2} x + 2\sin x \cos x = (\sin x + \cos x)^{2}\), so \(\sqrt{1 + \sin 2x} = |\sin x + \cos x| = \sin x + \cos x\) on \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\), where both terms are positive. Hence the integral is \(\left[\sin x - \cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi/4}\). At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) this is \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 0\) and at \(x = 0\) it is \(0 - 1 = -1\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(0 - (-1) = 1\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the key gives \(3\pi/16\), which is exactly \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{4}x\,dx\); the printed upper limit is \(\pi/4\), for which the value is \(3\pi/32-1/4=0.04452\). The key answers a different interval.]

Reduce the fourth power by repeated use of the half-angle formula: \(\sin^{4} x = \left(\dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1 - 2\cos 2x + \cos^{2} 2x}{4} = \dfrac{3 - 4\cos 2x + \cos 4x}{8}\). Integrating term by term, \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \sin^{4} x \, dx = \dfrac{1}{8}\left[3x - 2\sin 2x + \dfrac{\sin 4x}{4}\right]_{0}^{\pi/4}\). At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) the bracket is \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4} - 2 + 0\), and at \(x = 0\) it is \(0\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{3\pi}{32} - \dfrac{1}{4} \approx 0.04452\).

Complete the square in the denominator: \(x^{2} + 4x + 13 = (x + 2)^{2} + 3^{2}\). Using \(\int \dfrac{dx}{u^{2} + a^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{u}{a}\), the integral is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\left[\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x + 2}{3}\right]_{-4}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{4}{3} - \tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{4}{3} + \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\). The two arctangents combine, since \(\dfrac{\frac{4}{3} + \frac{2}{3}}{1 - \frac{8}{9}} = 18\) and the sum is acute. \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\tan^{-1} 18 \approx 0.5051\).

This integral is improper at BOTH endpoints, since the integrand is unbounded as \(x \to 0^{+}\) and as \(x \to 4^{-}\), but it converges, so it must be evaluated as a limit. Completing the square gives \(4x - x^{2} = 4 - (x - 2)^{2}\), so the antiderivative is \(\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x - 2}{2}\) and \(\int_{0}^{4} \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{4x - x^{2}}} = \lim_{a \to 0^{+}} \lim_{b \to 4^{-}} \left[\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x - 2}{2}\right]_{a}^{b}\). The bracket tends to \(\sin^{-1}(1) - \sin^{-1}(-1) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), both limits being finite. \(\therefore\) the value is \(\pi \approx 3.142\).

Complete the square under the radical: \(3 + 2x - x^{2} = 4 - (x - 1)^{2}\), which is positive on \([0, 1]\), so the integrand is continuous there. Using \(\int \dfrac{du}{\sqrt{a^{2} - u^{2}}} = \sin^{-1}\dfrac{u}{a}\), the integral is \(\left[\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x - 1}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}\). At \(x = 1\) this is \(\sin^{-1} 0 = 0\) and at \(x = 0\) it is \(\sin^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.5236\).

Integrate by parts taking \(u = x\) and \(dv = \sin x \, dx\), so that \(du = dx\) and \(v = -\cos x\). Then \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2} x \sin x \, dx = \left[-x\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} + \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos x \, dx = \left[-x\cos x + \sin x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}\). At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) the bracket is \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}(0) + 1 = 1\), and at \(x = 0\) it is \(0\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(1\).

Integrate by parts with \(u = \tan^{-1} x\) (the inverse-trigonometric factor) and \(dv = x \, dx\), giving \(v = \dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\). Then \(\int_{0}^{1} x \tan^{-1} x \, dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\tan^{-1} x\right]_{0}^{1} - \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x^{2}}{1 + x^{2}} dx = \dfrac{\pi}{8} - \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\right) dx\). The remaining integral is \(\left[x - \tan^{-1} x\right]_{0}^{1} = 1 - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{\pi}{8} - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2} \approx 0.2854\).

This integral is improper at the upper limit, so evaluate it over \([0, b]\) and let \(b \to \infty\). Integrating by parts with \(u = x\) and \(dv = e^{-x} dx\) gives \(\int_{0}^{b} x e^{-x} dx = \left[-x e^{-x}\right]_{0}^{b} + \int_{0}^{b} e^{-x} dx = \left[-(x + 1)e^{-x}\right]_{0}^{b} = 1 - (b + 1)e^{-b}\). Since the exponential beats the linear factor, \((b + 1)e^{-b} \to 0\) as \(b \to \infty\), so the integral converges. \(\therefore\) the value is \(1\).

Put \(x = \sin\theta\), so \(dx = \cos\theta \, d\theta\), \(\sin^{-1} x = \theta\) and \((1 - x^{2})^{3/2} = \cos^{3}\theta\); the limits \(x = 0\) and \(x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) become \(\theta = 0\) and \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). The integral becomes \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \theta \sec^{2}\theta \, d\theta\), which by parts (\(u = \theta\), \(dv = \sec^{2}\theta \, d\theta\)) equals \(\left[\theta\tan\theta\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} - \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \tan\theta \, d\theta\). Here \(\left[\theta\tan\theta\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\tan\theta \, d\theta = \left[-\log|\cos\theta|\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\log 2\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\log 2 \approx 0.4388\).

The presence of \(\sec^{2} x \, dx\) alongside \(\tan x\) invites the substitution \(t = \tan x\), \(dt = \sec^{2} x \, dx\), with limits \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\). The integral becomes \(\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{dt}{3t^{2} + 4t + 1} = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{dt}{(3t + 1)(t + 1)}\), and partial fractions give \(\dfrac{1}{(3t + 1)(t + 1)} = \dfrac{3}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{3t + 1} - \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{t + 1}\). Integrating, this is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\log\dfrac{3t + 1}{t + 1}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log 2 - \log 1\right)\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\log 2 \approx 0.3466\).

Rewrite the denominator in terms of \(\cos 2x\): \(\sin^{4} x + \cos^{4} x = 1 - 2\sin^{2} x \cos^{2} x = 1 - \dfrac{\sin^{2} 2x}{2} = \dfrac{1 + \cos^{2} 2x}{2}\). Now substitute \(t = \cos 2x\), so \(\sin 2x \, dx = -\dfrac{dt}{2}\), and the limits \(x = 0\) to \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) become \(t = 1\) to \(t = 0\). The integral becomes \(\int_{1}^{0} \dfrac{2}{1 + t^{2}}\left(-\dfrac{dt}{2}\right) = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{dt}{1 + t^{2}} = \left[\tan^{-1} t\right]_{0}^{1}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.7854\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the key gives 0, but the integrand is strictly positive on the interior so the integral cannot vanish. The value is \(8/21=0.38095\). The book appears to have SWAPPED this key with the one printed at Ex 4.2 III (6), where 8/21 is printed instead.]

Since \(\sin x\) occurs to an odd power, substitute \(t = \cos x\), \(dt = -\sin x \, dx\), and write \(\sin^{3} x \, dx = \sin^{2} x \cdot \sin x \, dx = -(1 - t^{2})\, dt\); the limits \(x = 0\) to \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) become \(t = 1\) to \(t = 0\). The integral becomes \(\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt{t}\,(1 - t^{2})\, dt = \int_{0}^{1}\left(t^{1/2} - t^{5/2}\right) dt = \left[\dfrac{2}{3}t^{3/2} - \dfrac{2}{7}t^{7/2}\right]_{0}^{1}\). Substituting the limits gives \(\dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac{2}{7}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{8}{21} \approx 0.3810\).

Use the half-angle (Weierstrass) substitution \(t = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}\), for which \(\cos x = \dfrac{1 - t^{2}}{1 + t^{2}}\) and \(dx = \dfrac{2\,dt}{1 + t^{2}}\); the limits \(x = 0\) to \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) become \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\). The denominator becomes \(5 + \dfrac{4(1 - t^{2})}{1 + t^{2}} = \dfrac{9 + t^{2}}{1 + t^{2}}\), so the integral reduces to \(\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{2\,dt}{9 + t^{2}} = \dfrac{2}{3}\left[\tan^{-1}\dfrac{t}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{2}{3}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.2145\).

Substitute \(t = \sin x\), \(dt = \cos x \, dx\), with limits \(t = 0\) to \(t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), reducing the integral to \(\int_{0}^{1/\sqrt{2}} \dfrac{dt}{4 - t^{2}}\). Using \(\int \dfrac{dt}{a^{2} - t^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2a}\log\left|\dfrac{a + t}{a - t}\right|\) with \(a = 2\), this is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\left[\log\dfrac{2 + t}{2 - t}\right]_{0}^{1/\sqrt{2}}\). The lower limit contributes \(\log 1 = 0\), and at \(t = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) the ratio is \(\dfrac{2 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{2 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{2\sqrt{2} - 1}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{1}{4}\log\dfrac{2\sqrt{2} + 1}{2\sqrt{2} - 1} \approx 0.1847\).

Substitute \(t = \sin x\), \(dt = \cos x \, dx\), with limits \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\), giving \(\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{dt}{(1 + t)(2 + t)}\). Partial fractions give \(\dfrac{1}{(1 + t)(2 + t)} = \dfrac{1}{1 + t} - \dfrac{1}{2 + t}\), so the integral is \(\left[\log\dfrac{1 + t}{2 + t}\right]_{0}^{1}\). At \(t = 1\) this is \(\log\dfrac{2}{3}\) and at \(t = 0\) it is \(\log\dfrac{1}{2}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\log\dfrac{2}{3} - \log\dfrac{1}{2} = \log\dfrac{4}{3} \approx 0.2877\).

Multiply numerator and denominator by \(e^{x}\) to clear the negative exponential: the integrand becomes \(\dfrac{e^{x}}{a^{2}e^{2x} + b^{2}}\), which suggests \(t = e^{x}\), \(dt = e^{x} dx\), with limits \(t = e^{-1}\) to \(t = e\). The integral becomes \(\int_{1/e}^{e} \dfrac{dt}{a^{2}t^{2} + b^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{a^{2}}\int_{1/e}^{e} \dfrac{dt}{t^{2} + \left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{ab}\left[\tan^{-1}\dfrac{at}{b}\right]_{1/e}^{e}\), assuming \(a\) and \(b\) are both non-zero. \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{1}{ab}\left[\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{ae}{b}\right) - \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{a}{be}\right)\right]\); for example, with \(a = 2\) and \(b = 3\) this is \(\approx 0.1377\).

Use the half-angle substitution \(t = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}\), with \(\sin x = \dfrac{2t}{1 + t^{2}}\), \(\cos x = \dfrac{1 - t^{2}}{1 + t^{2}}\) and \(dx = \dfrac{2\,dt}{1 + t^{2}}\); the limits \(x = 0\) to \(x = \pi\) become \(t = 0\) to \(t \to \infty\). The denominator becomes \(\dfrac{3(1 + t^{2}) + 4t + (1 - t^{2})}{1 + t^{2}} = \dfrac{2t^{2} + 4t + 4}{1 + t^{2}}\), so the integral reduces to \(\int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{dt}{t^{2} + 2t + 2} = \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{dt}{(t + 1)^{2} + 1} = \left[\tan^{-1}(t + 1)\right]_{0}^{\infty}\). This equals \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.7854\).

Peel off one \(\sec^{2} x\) as the differential: \(\sec^{4} x \, dx = \left(1 + \tan^{2} x\right)\sec^{2} x \, dx\), and put \(t = \tan x\), \(dt = \sec^{2} x \, dx\), with limits \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\). The integral becomes \(\int_{0}^{1}\left(1 + t^{2}\right) dt = \left[t + \dfrac{t^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}\). Substituting the limits gives \(1 + \dfrac{1}{3}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{4}{3} \approx 1.333\).

Rationalise by multiplying numerator and denominator inside the radical by \(1 - x\): \(\sqrt{\dfrac{1 - x}{1 + x}} = \dfrac{1 - x}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\), so the integral splits as \(\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}} - \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x \, dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\) (each piece is improper at \(x = 1\) but convergent, and their sum is the original integrand, which is continuous on \([0, 1]\)). The first is \(\left[\sin^{-1} x\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and the second, by \(u = 1 - x^{2}\), is \(\left[-\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\right]_{0}^{1} = 1\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1 \approx 0.5708\).

Since \(\sin x\) appears to an odd power, substitute \(t = \cos x\), \(dt = -\sin x \, dx\), and write \(\sin^{3} x \, dx = -(1 - t^{2})\, dt\); the limits \(x = 0\) to \(x = \pi\) become \(t = 1\) to \(t = -1\), and the integral becomes \(\int_{-1}^{1} (1 - t^{2})(1 + 2t)(1 + t)^{2} dt\). Now put \(u = 1 + t\) (so \(1 - t = 2 - u\) and \(1 + 2t = 2u - 1\), with \(u\) running from \(0\) to \(2\)), giving \(\int_{0}^{2} u^{3}(2 - u)(2u - 1)\, du = \int_{0}^{2}\left(-2u^{5} + 5u^{4} - 2u^{3}\right) du\). Evaluating, \(\left[-\dfrac{u^{6}}{3} + u^{5} - \dfrac{u^{4}}{2}\right]_{0}^{2} = -\dfrac{64}{3} + 32 - 8\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{8}{3} \approx 2.667\).

Write \(\sin 2x \, dx = 2\sin x \cos x \, dx\) and substitute \(t = \sin x\), \(dt = \cos x \, dx\), with limits \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\); the integral becomes \(\int_{0}^{1} 2t \tan^{-1} t \, dt\). Integrating by parts with \(u = \tan^{-1} t\) and \(dv = 2t \, dt\) gives \(\left[t^{2}\tan^{-1} t\right]_{0}^{1} - \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{t^{2}}{1 + t^{2}} dt = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \int_{0}^{1}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1 + t^{2}}\right) dt\). The remaining integral is \(\left[t - \tan^{-1} t\right]_{0}^{1} = 1 - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \left(1 - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1 \approx 0.5708\).

Put \(\theta = \cos^{-1} x\), so that \(\sin^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\) and \(\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}} = -d\theta\); the limits \(x = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(x = 1\) become \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\theta = 0\), and the sign from \(-d\theta\) flips them back. The integral becomes \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} e^{\theta}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) d\theta\). Here \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} e^{\theta} d\theta = e^{\pi/4} - 1\) and, by parts, \(\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \theta e^{\theta} d\theta = \left[(\theta - 1)e^{\theta}\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)e^{\pi/4} + 1\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\left(e^{\pi/4} - 1\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 1\right)e^{\pi/4} - 1 = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + 1\right)e^{\pi/4} - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 1\right) \approx 1.345\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the key gives \(\sin(\log 3)\), dropping the lower-limit contribution. With the printed lower limit 2 the value is \(\sin(\log 3)-\sin(\log 2)=0.25162\), not 0.89058.]

The factor \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) is exactly the derivative of \(\log x\), so substitute \(u = \log x\), \(du = \dfrac{dx}{x}\); the limits \(x = 2\) and \(x = 3\) become \(u = \log 2\) and \(u = \log 3\). The integral becomes \(\int_{\log 2}^{\log 3} \cos u \, du = \left[\sin u\right]_{\log 2}^{\log 3}\). \(\therefore\) the value is \(\sin(\log 3) - \sin(\log 2) \approx 0.2516\).
